docs.title: TPE Disk Image Processing
docs.text:
This pipeline automates the full analysis workflow of a 2D granular experiment using photoelastic disks — from raw experimental images to a complete force network. It combines deep learning (StarDist, ResNet) with physics-based optimization under mechanical equilibrium constraints.

Why this pipeline?

Wet photoelastic disks inevitably develop residual stress, which renders the classical \(G^2\) method unreliable. The custom-trained neural networks here are designed to work around this limitation.

Raw experimental image

Reconstructed from extracted positions & forces

docs.title: Workflow Overview
docs.text:
The pipeline consists of three main steps, each implemented as a Jupyter notebook. Each step results in a pickle file .pkl that stores a Pandas dataframe. The outputs of one step are the inputs to the next.

flowchart TD
    I1[Green Images] --> B[01. TPE_disk_tracking_stardist.ipynb]
    I2[UV Image] --> B
    I3[PE Image] --> B
    B --> C[Trajectory .pkl\n positions · angles · IDs · G²]
    C --> D[02. TPE_contact_detect.ipynb]
    D --> E[Contact Bond .pkl\n pairs · positions · angles]
    E --> F[03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb]
    F --> G[Force .pkl\n magnitudes & angles of contact forces]

    style I1 stroke:#4CAF50,stroke-width:3px
    style I2 stroke:#2196F3,stroke-width:3px
    style I3 stroke:#FFC107,stroke-width:3px
    style C stroke:#FFA726,stroke-width:2px
    style E stroke:#FFA726,stroke-width:2px
    style G stroke:#FFA726,stroke-width:2px
    style B stroke:#9C27B0,stroke-width:2px
    style D stroke:#9C27B0,stroke-width:2px
    style F stroke:#9C27B0,stroke-width:2px
Step Notebook Environment Output 1 01. TPE_disk_tracking_stardist.ipynb stardist_env Trajectory .pkl 2 02. TPE_contact_detect.ipynb torch_env Contact bond .pkl 3 03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb torch_env Force .pkl 3 (CPU) 03. TPE_solve_force_vector_CPU.ipynb torch_env Force .pkl (no GPU required)

For batch/automated runs across many experiments, see the Batch Script page.

docs.title: Finding Orientation Angles
docs.text:
Disk orientation is determined by analyzing the blue channel image, which contain a fluorescent line on each disk. The process is automated in the compute_frame_orientations function. Below briefly describr the workflow:

  1. Crop a patch around each detected disk centroid in the blue channel image.
  2. Threshold the patch to get rid of background noise and isolate the marker pixels.
  3. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is applied via orientation_weighted_pca to the marker pixels to find the major axis, which gives the disk's rotation angle \(\theta\).

This angle is stored in the output dataframe for each particle and frame.

To avoid a pi degeneracy, the angles are defined using the compute_continuous_angles function, such that the orientation rotates continuously from frame to frame, without any sudden jumps between 0 and pi. This is done by comparing the two possible angles (\(\theta\) and \(\theta+\pi\)) to the previous frame's \(\theta\), and choosing the one that is closer.

docs.title: Batch Script — run_pipeline.py
docs.text:
run_pipeline.py automates Steps 1 and 2 (disk tracking + contact detection) for one or more experiment directories from the command line.

Note

Step 3 (force vector computation) is currently notebook-only and is not included in this batch script.

docs.title: Single experiment
docs.text: python run_pipeline.py --img-dir "N:\PROJ_TPE\TPE_20260429A03_N=262x2_e-5rps"

docs.title: Multiple experiments (PowerShell loop)
docs.text:
$dirs = @(
    "N:\PROJ_TPE\TPE_20260429A01_N=262x2_e-5rps",
    "N:\PROJ_TPE\TPE_20260429A03_N=262x2_2e-5rps"
)
foreach ($d in $dirs) {
    python run_pipeline.py --img-dir $d --verbose
}

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Default Description --img-dir (required) Full path to the experiment image directory --pkl-dir M:\Archive\Proj_TPE\Disk_traj_files Output directory for trajectory .pkl files --bond-dir M:\Archive\Proj_TPE\Contact_bond_files Output directory for contact bond .pkl files --roi Y_MIN Y_MAX X_MIN X_MAX 250 1200 0 2000 Region of interest in pixels --d-tol 10 Neighbour distance tolerance (pixels) for contact search --verbose False Save diagnostic figures alongside the output .pkl files --skip-tracking False Skip Step 1; requires a trajectory .pkl to already exist --skip-contact False Skip Step 2; run tracking only

docs.title: Direct-run mode (no CLI flags)
docs.text:
For running directly from VS Code with "Run Python File", edit the constants near the top of run_pipeline.py:

DIRECT_RUN_IMG_DIR = [
    r"N:\PROJ_TPE\TPE_20260509A01_N=262x2_e-5rps_2e-2fps_1000frames",
    r"N:\PROJ_TPE\TPE_20260510A_N=262x2_6SpeedSweep_REVERSE_strain=0.5_5e2FramesEach",
]

DIRECT_RUN_VERBOSE        = True
DIRECT_RUN_SKIP_TRACKING  = False  # set True to reuse existing .pkl
DIRECT_RUN_SKIP_CONTACT   = False

When the script is launched with no CLI arguments it reads these values instead of using argparse.

docs.title: Camera calibration
docs.text:
The script applies a homography correction to align the green and PE image coordinate systems. The calibration matrix is stored at the top of run_pipeline.py:

CALIB_DATE = '2026-05-11'
DEFAULT_CALIB_H = np.array([
    [ 1.00897850e+00,  2.09385077e-02, -1.22728762e+00],
    [-1.80085815e-02,  1.01619232e+00, -4.11885450e+01],
    [-2.43424373e-06,  8.55305735e-07,  1.00000000e+00],
])

Replace the nine values when recalibrating the optical setup.

docs.title: Training Contact Detection (Step 2 Classifier)
docs.text:
This page documents how to train the contact-detection CNN used in Step 2. The training workflow is based on:

  • https://github.com/linjunJR/TPE_contact_detect_trainer

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The model is a binary classifier that predicts whether a contact ROI contains a true disk-disk contact:

  • class 0: no contact
  • class 1: contact

In the main pipeline, this model is used after geometric candidate generation to remove false positives.

docs.title: Repository workflow
docs.text:
The trainer repo uses a three-stage data-to-model process:

  1. Crop ROIs
  2. Notebook: Crop_contactROI_forTraining.ipynb
  3. Inputs: raw TPE frames plus bond/geometry metadata.

  4. Output: contact-centered cropped images.

  5. Label ROIs

  6. Notebook: Label_GUI_contact_detect.ipynb
  7. Interactive labeling into class folders (0/1).

  8. Includes optional random-rotation augmentation while saving.

  9. Train ResNet18

  10. Notebook: contact_detect_training_resnet.ipynb
  11. Two-phase transfer learning with warmup then fine-tuning.

docs.title: Model architecture
docs.text:
The trainer uses an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 backbone.

  • Backbone: ResNet18 (pretrained)
  • Input: 128 x 128 RGB, ImageNet-normalized
  • Head:
  • Linear(512 -> 1024)
  • ReLU
  • Dropout(0.5)
  • Linear(1024 -> 2)

Loss function:

  • CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)

docs.title: Data split and batching
docs.text:
From the training notebook/README:

  • Train/validation split: 80/20
  • Random seed for split: 42
  • Batch size: 32

The notebook caches loaded images in RAM before splitting (TensorDataset), which speeds training but needs adequate memory.

docs.title: Phase 1: Warmup
docs.text:
• Freeze backbone parameters.
  • Train only the classification head.
  • Optimizer: Adam on head parameters.
  • Typical LR: 1e-3.
  • Up to 200 epochs with early stopping (patience 20 in notebook).
  • Best checkpoint saved (validation-loss based).

docs.title: Phase 2: Fine-tuning
docs.text:
• Unfreeze full network.
  • Continue from best warmup checkpoint.
  • Lower LR for full-network optimization (notebook uses 1e-6).
  • Up to 200 epochs with early stopping.
  • Save best fine-tuned checkpoint.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The final deliverable is a trained classifier checkpoint (.pth) that can be loaded by the contact-detection inference code in Step 2.

Typical repo output paths:

  • warmup checkpoint (example): contact_detect_warmup.pth
  • fine-tuned checkpoint (example): contact_detect_finetuned.pth

docs.title: Recommended training procedure for your pipeline
docs.text:
1. Build a balanced ROI dataset from your own experiments.
  2. Verify labels carefully around near-touching disks (hard negatives).
  3. Run warmup to convergence, then fine-tune.
  4. Evaluate false positives/false negatives on held-out frames from unseen experiments.
  5. Export the best checkpoint and update your Step 2 model path.

docs.title: Practical notes
docs.text:
• Keep preprocessing consistent between training and inference (ROI size, grayscale-to-RGB conversion, normalization).
  • If recall is low, add more positive contacts and hard-negative examples.
  • If precision is low, increase hard-negative coverage and review GUI labels for ambiguous boundary cases.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Trainer repository: https://github.com/linjunJR/TPE_contact_detect_trainer
  • Main pipeline docs: step2-contact.md, contact-detect.md

docs.title: Contact Detection
docs.text:
Contact detection is performed in two stages:

  1. Neighbour search: For each frame, all pairs of particles within a distance threshold are considered as candidate contacts.

The distance threshold is typically \(r_i + r_j + d_{tol}\), where \(r_i\) and \(r_j\) are the radii of the two disks. \(d_{tol}\) is set to 10 pixels for reasonable performance. Larger \(d_{tol}\) would increase samples to classify and thus runtime, but smaller \(d_{tol}\) might miss some contacts.

After locating all the ij pairs, the code handles the index:

  • Disks on the boundary are marked with boundary=True, and these disks can only be the j disk in a contact pair (i.e. they can only be contacted by interior disks, not contact other disks). Hence, there is also no contacts between two boundary disks.

  • Each \(ij\) pair is only counted once to minimize the classification workload.

  • CNN classification: Each candidate contact patch is cropped from the image:

on the right is a contact, while on the left is a non-contact. These patches are then passed through a trained convolutional neural network (ResNet) to classify as contact or non-contact.

  • Only contacts above a certain confidence threshold are kept.

The output is a dataframe listing all detected contacts for each frame.

docs.title: Training Contact Force Initial Guess (CNN Regressor)
docs.text:
This page documents training for the force-initialization CNN used before inverse fitting in Step 3. The workflow is based on:

  • https://github.com/linjunJR/TPE_contact_force_CNN_trainer

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
For each contact ROI, the regressor predicts:

  • force magnitude
  • force angle

These predictions are used as warm-start values (force_pred, angle_pred) before physics-constrained optimization in the force solver.

docs.title: Data generation pipeline
docs.text:
Because labeled real data is limited, the repo trains primarily from synthetic data with known ground-truth force vectors.

Primary notebooks:

  1. Contact_force_regression_label_produce.ipynb
  2. Rotates each disk image so the target contact is aligned.
  3. Crops one contact-centered patch per contact.

  4. Saves numbered images plus a labels.npy file.

  5. Contact_force_regression_TRAINING.ipynb

  6. Loads cropped images and [force, angle] labels.
  7. Trains a two-output ResNet18 regressor (warmup + fine-tune).

Expected dataset format:

<output_dir>/
    00001.png ... NNNNN.png
    labels.npy      # shape (N, 2): [force_magnitude, force_angle]

docs.title: Model architecture
docs.text:
The model in the training notebook matches your pipeline-side definition (src/force.py):

  • Backbone: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18
  • Head:
  • Linear(512 -> 256)
  • ReLU
  • Dropout(0.2)
  • Linear(256 -> 2)

Input transform:

  • resize to 224 x 224
  • grayscale to 3 channels
  • ImageNet normalization

Output:

  • two regression targets: [force_magnitude, force_angle]

Loss decomposition:

  • MSE(force) + MSE(angle)

docs.title: Train/val/test split
docs.text:
From training notebook defaults:

  • train: 70%
  • validation: 15%
  • test: 15%

The notebook reports separate force and angle errors during train and validation, in addition to total loss.

docs.title: Phase 1: Warmup (frozen backbone)
docs.text:
• Freeze all ResNet backbone layers.
  • Train only regression head.
  • Optimizer: Adam.
  • LR: 1e-4.
  • Early stopping monitors validation loss.

Typical defaults from notebook:

  • epochs: 100
  • patience: 20
  • min_delta: 0.001

docs.title: Phase 2: Fine-tuning (full network)
docs.text:
• Reload best warmup checkpoint.
  • Unfreeze all layers.
  • Continue training with lower LR.
  • Optimizer: Adam.
  • LR: 1e-5.
  • Early stopping on validation loss.

Typical defaults from notebook:

  • epochs: 200
  • patience: 20
  • min_delta: 0.0001

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The trainer evaluates on held-out test data with:

  • force true-vs-pred scatter (typically log-log)
  • angle true-vs-pred scatter
  • loss curves across warmup and fine-tuning

The final checkpoint is then copied into your pipeline model folder (for example under models/) and loaded by Step 3.

docs.title: How this connects to your Step 3 notebook
docs.text: In 03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb, the loaded model predicts force_pred and angle_pred for each contact ROI. Those values are only the initial guess; final forces are obtained by per-particle optimization and reciprocity symmetrization.

docs.title: Practical recommendations
docs.text:
1. Keep the exact same preprocessing in training and inference.
  2. Cover wide force ranges in synthetic data to avoid bias in low/high force tails.
  3. Include realistic image noise/contrast variation in synthetic generation if transfer to experiment is weak.
  4. Validate model quality by downstream fitting behavior, not only standalone MSE.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Trainer repository: https://github.com/linjunJR/TPE_contact_force_CNN_trainer
  • Force initial guess overview: force-guess.md
  • Force fitting stage: force-solve.md

docs.title: Contact Force Initial Guess
docs.text: This page documents the initial guess stage for contact force inversion. The model definition is in get_model in src/force.py.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
For each detected contact ROI, predict:

  • force magnitude (force_pred)
  • contact half-angle (angle_pred)

These predictions are used as warm-start variables for the physics-constrained optimizer.

docs.title: Model definition in src/force.py
docs.text:
get_model(device, output_dim=2) builds a ResNet18 regression network:

  1. Starts from ImageNet-pretrained resnet18.
  2. Freezes all backbone parameters (requires_grad = False).
  3. Replaces final FC layer with:
  4. Linear(num_ftrs, 256)
  5. ReLU()
  6. Dropout(0.2)
  7. Linear(256, output_dim)
  8. Moves model to target device.

With output_dim=2, outputs are interpreted as [force, angle].

docs.title: How this is used in Step 3 notebook
docs.text:
In 03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb, the workflow is:

  1. Build model with src.get_model(DEVICE).
  2. Load weights from models/Contact_Force_ResNet_*.pth.
  3. Set model.eval().
  4. Extract contact ROIs frame-by-frame.
  5. Run batched inference.
  6. Write predictions back to the bond table as force_pred, angle_pred.

Typical transform chain used before inference:

  • resize ROI to 224 x 224
  • replicate grayscale to 3 channels
  • ImageNet normalization

docs.title: Why warm start matters
docs.text: The inverse problem in Step 3 is non-convex. Starting from random (f, alpha) is slower and more likely to end in poor local minima. The ResNet guess usually puts the optimizer close to a physically plausible basin, improving both speed and stability.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• contact ROIs from detected i-j pairs
  • trained weight file

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• dataframe/pickle with one row per directed contact and columns including:
  • frame
  • i, j
  • force_pred
  • angle_pred

These columns are directly consumed by fit_one_particle_cpu / fit_one_particle_gpu in src/force.py.

docs.title: Fitting to Find Forces
docs.text: This page explains the force-fitting stage implemented in src/force.py. It covers synthetic image generation, loss terms, per-particle optimization, and ij/ji symmetrization.

docs.title: Main functions in code
docs.text:
• synth_img_pytorch_residue(...): generate synthetic PE disk image from (f, alpha, beta).
  • fit_disk_residue(...): optimize f and alpha for one disk.
  • fit_one_particle_cpu(...) / fit_one_particle_gpu(...): prepare one particle crop and run fitting.
  • symmetrize_forces(...): enforce reciprocal consistency using lower fitLoss side.

docs.title: 1. Synthetic image forward model
docs.text:
synth_img_pytorch_residue builds a disk grid and computes intensity with StressSolve_residue_torch.

Given force/angle vectors at all contacts on one particle:

  • f = [f_1, ..., f_z]
  • alpha = [\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_z]
  • beta = [\beta_1, ..., \beta_z]

it produces a synthetic PE image for that disk. The grid/mask is cached in _mesh_cache for speed.

docs.title: 2. Optimization variables and constraints
docs.text:
fit_disk_residue optimizes f0 and alpha0 with Adam.

At each iteration:

  1. Forces are projected positive by f0_pos = abs(f0).
  2. Synthetic image is generated from current variables.
  3. Total loss is computed as:
\[ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{img} + \mathcal{L}_{torque} + \mathcal{L}_{force} \]

docs.title: Image term
docs.text:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{img} = \operatorname{mean}\left( G(I_{synth}) - I_{photo} \right)^2 \]

where \(G(\cdot)\) is Gaussian blur (smooth_image, kernel size 3, sigma 1.0 in current code path).

docs.title: Torque equilibrium term
docs.text:
With weight \(w_\tau = 10^5\) in code:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{torque} = w_\tau\left(\sum_k \sin(\alpha_k)\, r_m\, f_k\right)^2 \]

docs.title: Net force equilibrium term
docs.text:
Define angle_term = alpha - beta + pi/2.

\[ \mathcal{L}_{force} = \left(\sum_k \cos(\text{angle\_term}_k) f_k\right)^2 + \left(\sum_k \sin(\text{angle\_term}_k) f_k\right)^2 \]

This penalizes non-zero resultant force components.

docs.title: 3. Convergence and stopping
docs.text:
fit_disk_residue stops when either:

  • n_iter reached, or
  • early stopping triggers: improvement below tol for patience consecutive checks, or
  • loss becomes NaN/Inf.

Returned values:

  • fitted force array
  • fitted alpha array
  • final scalar loss (fitLoss)
  • loss history list

docs.title: 4. Per-particle wrappers
docs.text:
fit_one_particle_cpu and fit_one_particle_gpu do the same scientific steps:

  1. Extract one particle crop using get_disk_img.
  2. Convert to grayscale float image.
  3. Read initial guesses from contact rows:
  4. force_pred
  5. angle_pred
  6. beta
  7. Run fit_disk_residue.
  8. Write fitted values back into dataframe columns:
  9. force
  10. alpha
  11. fitLoss

Particles with one or zero contacts are skipped (z <= 1).

docs.title: 5. ij/ji reciprocity correction
docs.text: Each directed contact (i, j) and (j, i) is fit separately. They are then reconciled by symmetrize_forces.

docs.title: What symmetrize_forces requires
docs.text:
Input dataframe must contain:

  • frame
  • i, j
  • force
  • alpha
  • fitLoss

docs.title: Selection rule
docs.text:
For each reciprocal pair in the same frame:

  • compare fitLoss(i,j) and fitLoss(j,i)
  • keep force/alpha from lower-loss side
  • assign that same chosen value to both directions

It also returns diagnostic comparison metrics (force_diff, normalized force diff, wrapped alpha diff).

docs.title: 6. Practical tuning knobs
docs.text:
Most useful fitting knobs (from notebook config and fit_disk_residue):

  • lr: Adam learning rate
  • n_iter: max iterations
  • tol, patience: early-stop sensitivity
  • fsigma: photoelastic constant
  • plot_every: debug visualization in sequential mode

Recommended workflow:

  1. Validate on a small frame subset.
  2. Inspect synthetic vs experimental image overlap.
  3. Check reciprocity diagnostics after symmetrization.
  4. Run full dataset once settings are stable.

docs.title: Finding \(G^2\)
docs.text: \(G^2\) is a measure of the mean squared gradient of the photoelastic image intensity, used as a proxy for local stress in each disk. The computation itself is trivial, but the key is to first mask out the bright rim from the fluids, which would otherwise dominate the gradient and obscure the stress information from the disks. Below are the steps to compute \(G^2\) for each disk in the PE image.

docs.title: How \(G^2\) is computed
docs.text:
1. To mask out the bright rim from the fluids, subtract Gaussian rings around particle centers using src.subtract_gaussian_rings. Below is an example of the masked image:

  2. Crop out each disk in the PE image and compute the squared gradient of the intensity (using compute_G2_map).

  3. Average the squared gradient values within the circular region of the disk to get a single \(G^2\) value for each disk. Write to the resulting dataframe.

docs.title: Simulating Residual Stresses
docs.text: This page explains the residual-stress term used in Step 3 force inversion. The implementation is in StressSolve_residue_torch in src/force.py.

docs.title: Where it appears in code
docs.text:
• src.force.StressSolve_residue_torch(...): builds total stress from contact forces plus residual stress, then maps stress to intensity.
  • src.force.synth_img_pytorch_residue(...): calls the stress solver with power=6 and fills a disk mask on a px x px grid.

docs.title: Contact-force stress term
docs.text:
For each pixel inside a disk and each contact, the solver computes a contribution to:

  • sigmaxx
  • sigmayy
  • sigmaxy

These come from vectorized contact geometry (f, alpha, beta) and are summed over contacts.

docs.title: Residual-stress model in the code
docs.text:
After contact stress is computed, an axisymmetric residual field is added in polar form.

Definitions used in StressSolve_residue_torch:

  • \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + \varepsilon}\)
  • \(\Theta = \operatorname{atan2}(x, y)\)
  • \(p =\) power (currently fixed to \(6\) by synth_img_pytorch_residue)

Residual coefficient:

\[ K_{res} = -\frac{f_\sigma}{\pi\,p\,r_m^p}\,\arcsin(1) = -\frac{f_\sigma}{2\,p\,r_m^p} \]

Residual radial and tangential stresses:

\[ \sigma_r^{res} = K_{res}(r_m^p - R^p) \] \[ \sigma_t^{res} = K_{res}(r_m^p - (p+1)R^p) \]

These are rotated into Cartesian components and added to contact stress:

\[ \sigma_{xx}^{tot} = \sigma_{xx} + \sigma_r^{res}\cos^2\Theta + \sigma_t^{res}\sin^2\Theta \] \[ \sigma_{yy}^{tot} = \sigma_{yy} + \sigma_r^{res}\sin^2\Theta + \sigma_t^{res}\cos^2\Theta \] \[ \sigma_{xy}^{tot} = \sigma_{xy} + (\sigma_r^{res} - \sigma_t^{res})\sin\Theta\cos\Theta \]

docs.title: Stress-to-intensity mapping
docs.text:
The code computes principal-stress difference magnitude:

\[ \Delta\sigma = \sqrt{(\sigma_{xx}^{tot}-\sigma_{yy}^{tot})^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^{tot\,2}} \]

Then intensity:

\[ I = \sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{f_\sigma}\Delta\sigma\right) \]

This is exactly what StressSolve_residue_torch returns (after nan_to_num safety cleanup).

docs.title: Practical meaning of parameters
docs.text:
• fsigma: photoelastic calibration scale; changes fringe density/intensity response.
  • rm: disk radius in the solver coordinate system.
  • power: controls radial profile shape of residual stress; currently fixed at 6.
  • eps: tiny positive number for numerical stability in division and square roots.

docs.title: Why this helps fitting
docs.text: Without a residual term, the optimizer may force contact vectors to explain background/internal disk fringes that are not contact-induced. Adding this term lets the model account for baseline stress structure, reducing bias in fitted contact forces.

docs.title: Setup & Installation
docs.text:
This pipeline currently contains two separate conda environments because TensorFlow 2.10 (needed by StarDist) and PyTorch 2.x use incompatible NumPy ABI versions.

The pipeline works with or without a CUDA-capable GPU. If intended for GPU use, watch your CUDA versions when installing — the provided environments/ YAML files are configured for NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA 11.2 (for TF) and CUDA 12.6 (for PyTorch). Versions may vary based on your machine and driver; check the CUDA compatibility and PyTorch CUDA support pages for guidance.

Without a compatible GPU, the pipeline will run in CPU mode but expect roughly 1.5X longer runtimes for the first two steps. The third step offers a CPU friendly version that is optimized for speed using parallelization.

Check out the StarDist Docs and PyTorch Docs for more details on GPU requirements and troubleshooting.

Environment Notebooks GPU backend Key packages stardist_env 01 — Disk tracking TF 2.10 + CUDA 11.2 TensorFlow-GPU, StarDist, CSBDeep, Trackpy torch_env 02, 03 — Contact detect & Force solve PyTorch + CUDA 12.6 PyTorch 2.6+cu126, Torchvision

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
stardist_envtorch_env
  • NVIDIA driver ≥ 450.80.02
  • CUDA 11.2 system libraries (installed automatically via cudatoolkit=11.2)
  • NVIDIA driver ≥ 525.0 (for CUDA 12.6)
  • No system CUDA install needed — PyTorch CUDA libraries are bundled in the pip wheel

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
cd environments/
conda env create -f stardist_env.yml
conda env create -f torch_env.yml

This will create both environments from the pinned environments/ YAML files.

docs.title: Kernel Selection in VS Code / JupyterLab
docs.text:
When opening a notebook, select the matching kernel from the top-right kernel picker:

Notebook Kernel 01. TPE_disk_tracking_stardist.ipynb stardist_env 02. TPE_contact_detect.ipynb torch_env 03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb torch_env 03. TPE_solve_force_vector_CPU.ipynb torch_env

docs.title: Required Models
docs.text:
The pre-trained models must be placed in the models/ folder before running:

models/
├── stardist_model/      ← StarDist2D model for disk segmentation (Notebook 01)
├── contact_model.pth    ← CNN contact classifier (Notebook 02)
└── force_model.pth      ← ResNet force regressor (Notebook 03)

Contact the authors if you need access to the pre-trained model weights.

docs.title: Train Your Own StarDist Model
docs.text:
This page summarizes the workflow used in:

  • manual_refine_GUI.ipynb
  • mask_generator.ipynb
  • TRAINING_stardist_disk_finder.ipynb

The training process has three stages:

  1. Manually refine disk centroids/radii in a tracking .pkl
  2. Convert refined tracks into instance masks
  3. Train and validate a StarDist2D model

docs.title: 1. Environment and folders
docs.text:
Use the stardist_env environment described in Setup.

Expected data layout (relative to stardist training and logistics/):

stardist_data/
  TPE_disk/
    train/
      images/
      masks/
stardist_models/

The training notebook expects matching filenames in images/ and masks/.

docs.title: 2. Refine trajectories manually (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
Notebook: manual_refine_GUI.ipynb

Purpose: correct missed or incorrect disk detections before generating masks.

docs.title: What to set
docs.text:
• pickle_file: input/output trajectory file
  • frame_files: image sequence path (for example Ic_*.png)
  • roi: crop region
  • camera_align(...): homography matrix for your current optical setup
  • frame_idx: starting frame for editing

docs.title: Controls in the GUI
docs.text:
• Left click: add small disk
  • Right click: add large disk
  • d: delete mode, then click a disk to remove
  • Left/Right arrow: move frames (step size is 5 in the notebook)
  • s: save

The notebook writes the corrected dataframe back to the same .pkl.

docs.title: 3. Generate training masks from refined .pkl
docs.text:
Notebook: mask_generator.ipynb

Purpose: create paired image/mask files for StarDist instance segmentation.

docs.title: What to set
docs.text:
• pickle_path: refined trajectory file
  • circle_img_dir: folder containing input circle/green-channel images
  • suffix: filename suffix to prevent collisions across experiments
  • for frame in [...]: frames to export
  • save and plot:
  • first run with save = 0, plot = 1 for visual check
  • then run with save = 1 to write files

docs.title: Important preprocessing in this notebook
docs.text:
• camera_align(...) applies perspective correction
  • roi crops the field of view
  • f['x'] = f['x'] - 100 trims the left boundary to match cropped images
  • each disk gets a unique instance ID in the output mask (uint16)

Outputs are written to:

  • stardist_data/TPE_disk/train/images/*.tif
  • stardist_data/TPE_disk/train/masks/*.tif

Use identical filenames for each image-mask pair.

docs.title: 4. Train StarDist2D
docs.text: Notebook: TRAINING_stardist_disk_finder.ipynb

docs.title: 4.1 Load and check data
docs.text:
The notebook:

  • reads *.tif from images/ and masks/
  • asserts image and mask filenames match
  • converts images to grayscale with I[:,:,0]
  • normalizes each image with normalize(x, 1, 99.8, axis=(0,1))
  • fills tiny label holes using fill_label_holes

Then it splits data with:

  • random seed: 42
  • validation fraction: 15% (minimum 1 image)

docs.title: 4.2 Augmentation used in your notebook
docs.text:
augmenter(x, y) applies:

  • random flips along spatial axes
  • intensity perturbation (* U(0.9,1.1) + U(-0.5,0.5))
  • Gaussian noise (sigma = 0.02 * U(0,1))

If needed, disable augmentation by passing augmenter=None in model.train.

docs.title: 4.3 Model configuration
docs.text:
Current defaults in your notebook:

  • n_rays = 32
  • grid = (4,4)
  • n_channel_in = 1
  • use_gpu = False and gputools_available()

grid = (4,4) is intentionally used to enlarge effective field of view and improve performance for your dense disk scenes.

docs.title: 4.4 Save location and training call
docs.text:
Your notebook creates a timestamped run folder and trains for 300 epochs:

from datetime import datetime
from stardist.models import StarDist2D

result_folder_name = datetime.now().strftime("%m-%d_%H-%M")
model = StarDist2D(conf, name=result_folder_name, basedir=r"C:\Users\jcTSAI\Desktop\stardist_models")
h = model.train(X_trn, Y_trn, validation_data=(X_val, Y_val), augmenter=augmenter, epochs=300)

Recommended adjustment: change basedir to your project folder, for example:

model = StarDist2D(conf, name=result_folder_name, basedir="stardist_models")

docs.title: 5. Optimize thresholds
docs.text:
After training, run:

model.optimize_thresholds(X_val, Y_val)

This selects:

  • prob_thresh: confidence threshold for keeping a candidate instance
  • nms_thresh: non-maximum suppression threshold for overlapping candidates

The optimized values are saved in thresholds.json inside the run folder.

docs.title: 6. Evaluate results
docs.text:
The notebook provides two checks:

  1. Overlay predictions on validation images
  2. Overlay predictions on a specific test frame (test_image_filename)

It also computes dataset metrics across IoU thresholds (tau = 0.1 ... 0.9):

  • precision, recall, accuracy, f1
  • mean scores and panoptic quality
  • TP/FP/FN counts

Use these plots to compare runs and pick your final model.

docs.title: 7. Reuse trained model in the pipeline
docs.text:
Each trained run folder contains files such as:

  • weights_best.h5
  • weights_last.h5
  • thresholds.json

Copy the selected model folder into your pipeline model location (for example models/stardist_model/) and point your disk-tracking step to that model.

docs.title: 8. Practical tips from this workflow
docs.text:
• Keep camera alignment and ROI consistent between mask generation and inference.
  • Use filename suffixes (for example _dense0919A01.tif) when mixing data from multiple experiments.
  • Start with quality over quantity: a smaller, clean, manually corrected set usually trains better than a large noisy set.
  • If predictions merge neighbors too often, check masks first, then adjust nms_thresh and retrain if needed.

docs.title: StarDist
docs.text:
StarDist is a deep learning model for object detection and segmentation, particularly well-suited for star-convex shapes like disks. In this pipeline, StarDist2D is used to detect and segment photoelastic disks in the green fluorescence channel images.

  • StarDist GitHub
  • StarDist paper

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: StarDist predicts a set of rays (distances from the center) for each object, allowing it to reconstruct the object boundary as a star-convex polygon. This is more robust than simple thresholding or circular Hough transforms, especially in crowded or noisy images.

docs.title: Usage in this pipeline
docs.text:
• Input: Green-channel images (green_*.png)

  • We camera_align the green image into our standard coordinate system before feeding it to StarDist.

  • The magic happens at 

       #PREDICT 
    mask, detail = model.predict_instances(input_image, n_tiles=model._guess_n_tiles(input_image), show_tile_progress=False)

The model returns a labelled mask object containing each pixel region detected as disk, and a unique integer label for each region. We then find the centroid of the region as the temporary disk center, and also obtain the eccentricity of each region to later filter out non-disk objects. Area is used duistinguish between large and small disks, to which we then manually assign a radius of 46 or 37 pixels, respectively.

# Compute properties
    props = measure.regionprops(mask)

    # Create a list of dicts
    for region in props:
        y, x = region.centroid  # note: (row, col) = (y, x)
        records.append({
            "frame": frame,
            "x": x,
            "y": y,
            "area": region.area,
            "ecc": region.eccentricity
        })
......

df_filtered = df[(df["x"] < 1860)&(df["x"] > 100)&(df["y"] > 50)] #trim off boundary 
df_filtered = df_filtered[df_filtered["ecc"] < 0.6] #filter eccentricity #ecc filter changed to 0.6 20250923
df_filtered.loc[:,'rpx'] = 46 #add radius column
df_filtered.loc[df_filtered['area']<6000, 'rpx'] = 37

The detected centroids are then linked into trajectories using Trackpy.

docs.title: Step 1 — Disk Tracking with StarDist
docs.text:
Notebook: 01. TPE_disk_tracking_stardist.ipynb Kernel: stardist_env

This notebook detects and tracks photoelastic disks across all frames using a pre-trained StarDist2D segmentation model, then computes orientation angles from the UV fluorescent image, and per-particle \(G^2\) values from the PE images as well.

Green channel — disk positions UV channel — orientation markers PE image — photoelastic fringes

docs.title: 1. Disk detection (StarDist2D)
docs.text: Each green-channel frame is fed to the StarDist2D model, which returns star-convex polygon instances for every disk. Centroids and radii (rpx) are extracted from the instance labels.

docs.title: 2. Particle linking (Trackpy)
docs.text: Detected centroids are linked across frames into trajectories using Trackpy. Short gaps (single missing frames) are filled by linear interpolation via interpolate_pos_angle.

docs.title: 3. Rotation angle via PCA
docs.text: For each detected disk in each frame, the UV-channel patch around the centroid is thresholded and the orientation marker is located. PCA on the marker pixels gives the disk rotation angle theta.

docs.title: 4. DoG Refinement of disk centers for improved tracking accuracy
5. Per-particle G²
docs.text: The PE image is cropped around each disk and the mean squared gradient (\(G^2\)) is computed as a proxy for stress magnitude.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
A single pickle file is saved containing a pandas.DataFrame with one row per (particle, frame) pair:

Column Description particle Unique particle ID frame Frame index x, y Centroid position (pixels) rpx Disk radius (pixels) angle Rotation angle (radians) g2 Per-particle \(G^2\) value boundary True if boundary particle

docs.title: Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
We choose the black-white camera as the standard frame of reference. So the first thing is to make sure is the camera calibration matrix looks alright. This is used to convert the perspective of the colored camera to the monochrome camera, so that we can track the disks in the green channel and then map those positions perfectly to the standard reference frame of the PE images.

So go ahead and run the first few cells. Remeber to change the IMG_DIR and EXP_FOLDER accordingly. After the tracking is done, check the diagnostic figures to make sure the tracking looks good:

Some red circles might look slightly off, which is fine. Just make sure there are no systematic shifts or scaling issues that points to a bad calibration. If that's the case, you must update the calibration matrix by redoing the chessboard calibration demonstrated in This notebook, and update the homography matrix in the camera_align function.

If you're lucky and the tracking looks good, move on to run the next cell that links the detected positions into trajectories. Here you have the option to track in separate segments if your experiment is not one continuous series of frames, but several trials that are filmed into one folder and should be tracked separately. Adjust the N_SEGMENTS and FRAMES_PER_SEG accordingly. The particle trajectories in different trials will not be continuous, and particle indices will be shifted by a large number between trials so ids aren't reused across trials. If your experiment is one continuous recording, just set N_SEGMENTS=1 and it will track all frames together.

From here on all the following cells can be run in one go. No input params needed. Just check the random diagnostic figures to make sure the angles and G² values look reasonable. If all looks good, you should have your trajectory pickle saved and we can move on to Step 2.

Check out the How-it-Works of Stardist, Angle detection, and G² calculation in the notebook for more details on the methods and algorithms.

docs.title: Step 2 — Contact Detection
docs.text:
Notebook: 02. TPE_contact_detect.ipynb Kernel: torch_env

This notebook identifies which particle pairs are in physical contact and classifies each candidate pair using a trained convolutional neural network (CNN).

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Variable Description PKL_FILE Path to the trajectory .pkl from Step 1 IMG_DIR Directory containing PE images (bw_*.png) D_TOL Distance tolerance in pixels for neighbour search (default: 10) Contact model Pre-trained CNN in models/contact_model.pth

docs.title: 1. Neighbour search
docs.text: For every frame, all pairs of particles whose centre-to-centre distance falls within \(r_i + r_j + D\_TOL\) pixels are enumerated as candidate contacts.

docs.title: 2. Contact patch extraction
docs.text: For each candidate pair \((i, j)\), a small image patch centred on the contact point is cropped from the PE image. The patch is rotated so the contact normal is always horizontal (canonical orientation).

docs.title: 3. CNN classification
docs.text:
The patch is passed through the pre-trained contact detection network (ResNet backbone). The network outputs a binary label:

  • 1 → confirmed contact
  • 0 → no contact (gap or near-miss)

along with a continuous confidence score.

docs.title: 4. Post-processing
docs.text: Low-confidence detections can be filtered by a threshold. The resulting contact list is deduplicated so each \((i, j)\) pair appears once per frame.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
A pickle file is saved containing a pandas.DataFrame with one row per (contact, frame):

Column Description frame Frame index i, j Particle IDs forming the contact xi, yi Position of particle \(i\) (pixels) xj, yj Position of particle \(j\) (pixels) beta Contact angle (radians, measured from the vertical) score CNN classification confidence

docs.title: Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
If step 1 is done correctly, theres not much that can go wrong here. The CNN model do all the work here. Just make sure to set the correct paths at the top of the notebook:

EXP_FOLDER = "TPE_20260518A03_N=262x2_step_shear_relax_e-3rpsx10s_stop100s_1fps_10reps"
TRAJ_DIR  = r'M:\Archive\Proj_TPE\Disk_traj_files'   # trajectory .pkl files
IMG_DIR   = r'N:\PROJ_TPE'                            # raw image root
BOND_DIR  = r'M:\Archive\Proj_TPE\Contact_bond_files' # output directory

Regardless, it is always good practice to first check by running only a few frames to check that nothing has gone wrong.

docs.title: Step 3 — Force Vector Computation
docs.text:
Notebook: 03. TPE_solve_force_vector.ipynb Kernel: torch_env

(A CPU-only variant 03. TPE_solve_force_vector_CPU.ipynb is also available for machines without a compatible GPU.)

This notebook computes the magnitude and direction of the contact force at each contact starting from a ResNet-based initial guess, and constrained optimization enforcing mechanical equilibrium.

docs.title: 1. Initial force guess (ResNet regression)
docs.text: For each contact region, the force regression model predicts an initial force magnitude and contact angle \(\alpha\). This gives a warm start for the optimizer.

docs.title: 2. Optimization with equilibrium constraints
docs.text: The force magnitudes and angles are refined by minimizing the pixel-wise difference between the synthetic and real PE images for each non-boundary particle. Also, net force and net torques on each grain are added as loss terms to guide the optimization towards physically consistent solutions.

docs.title: 3. Symmetrization
docs.text: Each contact \((i, j)\) is fit independently from particles \(i\) and \(j\). The symmetrize_forces function compares the two estimates and keeps the one with lower fit loss, enforcing Newton's third law.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Whats different from the previous two notebooks is that this step is extra time-consuming, so there are intermediate outputs designed in case of crashes or OOM errors. The initial prediction from the ResNet is saved as a PREDICTION pickle. During the optimization, results for each frame are saved in a temporary csv file once that frame is processed, and at the end of the notebook, these are aggregated into a final FORCE pickle file:

Column Description frame Frame index i, j Particle IDs force Contact force magnitude (N) alpha Half-contact-angle (radians) beta Contact normal angle (radians) fitLoss Residual image loss after optimization

docs.title: Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
If you follow standard dirctory conventions in the previous two steps, all you need to change is the EXP_NAME variable. Running the prediction cell would take roughly 1 hour for 2000 frames of 200 disks on a GPU.

After the prediction is done and saved as a preliminary pickle, go ahead and run the optimization procedure below. The cells look pretty intimidating but they are mostly just GPU configs and fallback safenets, so just run them as is. Again, start with one or few frames to make sure thing look reasonable. You can turn on the plot_every option in the config cell to visualize each grain and its fitted results, or you can view the full-field synthetic image of one frame by running one of the below cells. If fitting is failing and adjustment is needed, find more details in the "How it works" section.

Fitting would take about 40 seconds per frame on a GPU. After each frame is done, the results are immediately saved to a temporary csv file, so if the notebook crashes or runs out of memory, you can just restart it and it will pick up from the last saved frame. After all frames are done, the csv files are aggregated into a final pickle file. Optionally delete the temporary csv files or the prediction pickle file to save disk space.
